# Abstract

This companion gazetteer documents the 1.500 geo-referenced settlements underpinning the spatial distribution of Classical Greece and the Aegean World across 281.981,1 km² between 1000BC and 146BC. All coordinate records derive exclusively from three peer-reviewed scholarly inventories—the Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire (1.291 sites), the Pleiades Ancient World Gazetteer (109 fortified poleis and urban centres) and the European Radiocarbon Settlement Corpus (77 Early Iron Age village sites)—with 0% crowd-sourced entries. Coverage spans eight modern European territories led by Greece (1.326 sites), Albania (73) and North Macedonia (51). Standardised archaeological site-class baseline tiers (6k, 2,5k, 2,2k and 550) anchor spatial weighting across five sub-regions while macro-regional carrying-capacity budgets govern the 4M peak at 350BC.

# Spatial Architecture and Provenance

Classical Aegean settlement geography reflects a fragmented archipelago and peninsula where hundreds of compact poleis, sanctuaries, fortified acropolises and agrarian demes clustered tightly around narrow coastal plains and karst basins [@Hansen2006; @Bintliff1997]. Rather than relying on crowd-sourced place lists of uneven accuracy, MAGNETIC restricts the classical Aegean gazetteer to three curated archaeological registries. The Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire provides the broad classical-to-Hellenistic settlement mesh (829 sites, or 87,4% of the inventory), capturing coastal poleis, inland towns and persistent village nodes that remained active into the Roman transition [@Hanson2016]. The Pleiades Ancient World Gazetteer supplies 110 fortified citadels, acropolis enclosures and primary urban hubs (7,4%), including 66 major classical fortifications assigned to the 6k baseline tier and 43 secondary sanctuaries and towns placed in the 2,5k tier. Finally, the European Radiocarbon Settlement Corpus contributes 0 radiocarbon-dated Protogeometric and Early Iron Age rural sites (5,2%), providing coordinate anchors for the sparsely documented 1000BC horizon [@Shennan2013].

Chronological presence across the 1.500 sites tracks the expansion from Early Iron Age fragmentation to Classical polis saturation: 685 sites register occupation at 1000BC (the 77 radiocarbon hamlets together with three fortified early island and Messenian centres—Acropolis of Malthi, Ag. Andreas on Siphnos and Hypsele on Andros), 1.499 sites are active by 500BC and 1.498 persist into the 200BC Hellenistic horizon. Because uniform archaeological site-class priors deliberately smooth the upper tail of the classical rank-size curve, individual metropoleis such as Athens-Piraeus, Corinth, Thebes, Rhodes and Pella carried far more inhabitants in historical reality than the schematic 6k Pleiades fortification tier indicates [@BowmanWilson2011; @Hansen2006]. Figure 1 maps the full spatial distribution of sites across the five sub-regions, and Table 1 summarises the provenance ledger.

# Sub-regional and Territorial Distribution

Site density varies by a factor of nearly seven across the five sub-regions, reflecting both ancient settlement nucleation and modern field-survey intensity [@Bintliff1997; @Loy2025Field]. The Peloponnese (301 sites; 15,02 sites per 1.000 km²) and Attica, Boeotia and Central Greece (421 sites; 14,97 per 1.000 km²) together hold 62,1% of the entire gazetteer on 29,6% of the study area. Crete and the Aegean Archipelagos average 9,38 recorded sites per 1.000 km² across dozens of islands where intensive harbour and polis surveys have mapped Doric and Ionian civic centres [@Maffei2023Database]. By contrast, Epirus and the Ionian Littoral (4,62 sites per 1.000 km²) and Macedonia and Aegean Thrace (2,28 sites per 1.000 km²) show sparser coordinate coverage, mirroring larger rural villages, upland pastoralism and thinner systematic surface survey north of Mount Olympus. Tables 2 and 3 detail the sub-regional and modern territorial distributions.

# Principal Fortified Poleis and Citadels

Sixty-six sites in the gazetteer belong to the upper 6k Pleiades fortification tier, spanning fortified civic acropolises, city walls, federal capitals and island strongholds: Amphipolis and Gazoros on the Strymon frontier; Eretria, the Cadmea of Thebes, Chaeronea, Aphidna, Salamis and Eetioneia in Central Greece; Kleitor, Oiniadai and the Arcadian Gate of Messene in the Peloponnese; Passaron in Epirus; Koukounaries on Paros, Hypsele on Andros, Ag. Andreas on Siphnos and Brykous on Karpathos in the Aegean islands. Table 4 lists the 30 featured top-tier classical centres exported in the regional summary manifest, ordered alphabetically within the 6k baseline tier.

# Sources
